ai.definition: Orbital construction refers to the process of constructing large-scale structures in space, utilizing robotic systems and additive manufacturing techniques. These structures are often intended for long-term human habitation or industrial purposes.
ai.howItWorks: Advanced robotics and 3D printing technologies are employed to construct these structures using local materials sourced from asteroids or moons. This approach minimizes the need for transportation of construction materials from Earth, significantly reducing costs and environmental impact.
ai.problemSolved: Reduces the logistical challenges associated with building large-scale infrastructure in space, such as the high cost and complexity of transporting materials from Earth.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing and testing robotic systems capable of operating in microgravity environments. This includes creating specialized 3D printers and other construction tools that can function under these unique conditions.
ai.buildProcess: Structures are built layer by layer, starting with a base structure and gradually adding material until the desired shape is achieved. Local materials such as regolith (moon dust) or asteroid rock are processed into usable forms for printing.
ai.costDrivers: High initial investment in research and development of specialized equipment; ongoing costs related to maintaining robotic systems in space environments.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is still in the early stages of development but shows potential for significant advancements in future decades.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations governing orbital construction. However, international agreements such as the Outer Space Treaty may influence how this technology develops and is implemented.
ai.risks: Technological challenges related to operating in microgravity; environmental risks associated with asteroid mining or moon excavation; potential legal issues regarding resource extraction rights.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to high initial costs and lack of widespread commercial applications. Potential for significant long-term benefits if successful, particularly in reducing launch costs for space missions.
ai.futureDevelopment: Expected advancements in robotics, 3D printing technology, and materials science could drive further progress in this field. Collaboration between governments and private companies may accelerate development.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and processing of raw materials.

glossary.def: A process where three-dimensional objects are created by laying down successive layers of material until the desired object is formed.
An environment in which the effects of gravity are significantly reduced, typically found in space.
The layer of loose, heterogeneous material covering solid rock on terrestrial planets and some other Solar System bodies, such as asteroids or moons.

subsystems.name: Robotic assembly layer
subsystems.role: manipulates, positions and joins structural elements without crews.

subsystems.name: Feedstock supply
subsystems.role: delivers the mass to be built with — the hard part, since everything starts on Earth or must be mined off-world.
parts: asteroid or lunar material extraction (not yet realised)

subsystems.name: Fabrication unit
subsystems.role: turns raw material or stock into beams, panels and shells.
parts: additive manufacturing head (powder, wire or resin)

subsystems.name: Joining and structure
subsystems.role: locks pieces into one rigid body.

subsystems.name: Habitat envelope
subsystems.role: holds pressure and temperature for people or processes.

subsystems.name: Shielding and outfitting
subsystems.role: makes the volume survivable and usable.

buildSteps.title: Decide the orbit
buildSteps.detail: Pick an orbit low enough for launch and resupply but high enough that residual atmosphere does not drag down a very large structure over years.

buildSteps.title: Deliver feedstock and robots
buildSteps.detail: Launch stock, printer heads and arms as compact payloads, then rendezvous and dock them with a small tug or an existing platform.

buildSteps.title: Extend the skeleton
buildSteps.detail: Robotic arms latch truss segments end to end, using grapple fixtures and alignment guides rather than human hands, to build up a stiff backbone many tens of metres long.

buildSteps.title: Manufacture members in place
buildSteps.detail: Beams and panels are printed or pultruded in orbit from stock or, later, from refined regolith or metal, so only raw material has to be launched.

buildSteps.title: Join and rigidise
buildSteps.detail: Preloaded bolts, clamps, or welded and brazed seams lock the members together; welding in vacuum has been flown experimentally, but never at this scale.

buildSteps.title: Pressurise and test
buildSteps.detail: Inflatable or rigid shells are filled with air, then leak-tested, and the whole structure is checked for vibration and thermal distortion.

buildSteps.title: Shield and outfit
buildSteps.detail: Several metres of regolith, soil or water are piled around occupied volumes to approximate Earth's atmosphere as radiation shielding.

buildSteps.title: Commission and operate
buildSteps.detail: Power, thermal control and life support are brought online, and the facility begins its working life — science, manufacturing or habitation.

prerequisites.why: cargo and crew vehicles already dock themselves routinely, which is how building materials would arrive.
long arms and dexterous manipulators have assembled the ISS module by module, but not large truss structures autonomously.

prerequisites.tech: Additive manufacturing in vacuum and microgravity
prerequisites.why: plastic and metal printing have been demonstrated on the space station; printing with regolith or at structural scale has only been done in laboratories.
mining and processing asteroidal or lunar material has never been done; it is the only way to escape launch-cost limits.

prerequisites.tech: Closed-loop life support and radiation shielding
prerequisites.why: water and air are partly recycled on the space station, but a self-sufficient habitat needs far more closure and metre-scale shielding mass.

pathway.milestone: servicing and assembly demonstrations on and around the space station
pathway.unlocks: proven robotic grasping, refuelling interfaces and module joining.

pathway.milestone: robotic assembly of a large antenna or truss in orbit without crew
pathway.unlocks: confidence that big structures can be built from small launches.

pathway.milestone: off-world material processing demonstrated on the Moon, starting with oxygen and simple metal parts
pathway.unlocks: the first construction feedstock that does not come from Earth.

pathway.milestone: orbital yards building pressurised habitats and industrial facilities
pathway.unlocks: large-scale habitation, in-orbit manufacturing and ships assembled away from Earth's gravity.
